clinician.trajectory_summary: An 86-year-old woman with cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, angina pectoris, CKD) presented with sudden-onset abdominal pain, elevated serum phosphate, metabolic lactic acidosis, and leukocytosis suggesting acute mesenteric ischemia. Contrast-enhanced CT showed no signs of bowel ischemia or occlusion, excluding occlusive causes. Six hours after admission, exploratory laparotomy revealed discontinuous necrosis of the ileum and entire colon (except sigmoid) with preserved superior mesenteric artery pulsation and no bowel obstruction, confirming non-occlusive etiology. She underwent ileal resection, subtotal colectomy, and jejunostomy with 120 cm residual jejunum. Post-operatively, she recovered with immediate normalization of serum phosphate.
